methodology.title: Recommendation methodology
methodology.intro: Each recommendation is grounded in traceable data, personality and career-preference signals, and transparent scoring rules. This page explains how the system uses those inputs.

personality.heading: 01 · Personality and lifestyle assessment
personality.body: We use the Big Five model to understand your learning and lifestyle preferences. The assessment uses ten short questions. It does not diagnose you or label you; it helps the system judge whether theory-heavy, applied, or balanced programs are more suitable.
citations: Goldberg, L. R. (1990). An alternative "description of personality": The Big-Five factor structure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59(6), 1216-1229.
Costa, P. T., & McCrae, R. R. (1992). Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO PI-R) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI) professional manual. Psychological Assessment Resources.
Gosling, S. D., Rentfrow, P. J., & Swann, W. B. (2003). A very brief measure of the Big-Five personality domains (TIPI). Journal of Research in Personality, 37(6), 504-528.

career.heading: 02 · Career inclination and program field
career.body: Career fit references Holland's RIASEC model to compare your tendencies with fields such as computing, finance, design, and education. The system does not lock you into a career type. It treats this as one signal and combines it with your preferences around work, migration, returning home, internships, and salary.
citations: Holland, J. L. (1997). Making vocational choices: A theory of vocational personalities and work environments (3rd ed.). Psychological Assessment Resources.
Nauta, M. M. (2010). The development, evolution, and status of Holland's theory of vocational personalities. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 57(1), 11-22.

data.heading: 03 · Institution data: public sources + human review
data.body: Institution and program data comes only from public sources such as admissions pages, government datasets, and university publications. Every record needs a source link and verification date. Unsourced content is excluded, production data requires human review, and generated content is never allowed to invent institution facts.
citations: docs/data-pipeline.md — Ingest pipeline spec: fetch -> parse -> normalize -> Zod validate -> diff -> draft -> human promote.
docs/data-pipeline-sources.md — Source playbook: strict robots.txt, >=1 req/s per host, zero PII.
docs/spec.md FR-3.4 / FR-3.5 — Data governance: every row traceable, quarterly full re-verification.

scoring.heading: 04 · Scoring engine: weighted, not gated
scoring.body: The system does not rely on one filter. Unless you explicitly exclude a country or your grades are far below a program's requirement, recommendations are scored across academic fit, lifestyle, career direction, budget, program strengths, and reputation. Weights adjust when your preferences are clear, such as giving budget more influence when cost is a priority.
citations: docs/spec.md FR-4 — Scoring formula and personalization rules.
packages/core/src/rules/ — All scoring logic (one file per dimension, with unit tests).

ai.heading: 05 · Generated-content boundary
ai.body: Generative models only help with wording, extracting fields from uploaded material, and turning guided Q&A answers into preference signals. They do not create institution facts. Any information without a traceable source is filtered out before it can affect recommendations.
citations: docs/prohibition.md — Red line 2: no recommendation may be emitted without a source_id.
.github/instructions/ai-layer.instructions.md — All LLM outputs go through Zod validation and citation filtering.

closing.heading: Why so strict?
closing.body: Studying abroad is a high-cost decision. We would rather recommend fewer programs than include information whose source cannot be checked. The full specifications and change records are available in the repository's docs/ directory for review.
